questions.stem: In a survey write-up, the report states that the frog population halved and concludes that the new drainage scheme caused it. What is the warrant joining the claim to the reason?

options.text: Any change in frog numbers that follows the drainage works must have been caused by those works.
Frog populations are easy to count, so the halving recorded on site must be real.
options.misconception: treats a reason about counting as the connecting assumption

options.text: The drainage scheme was built by the same trust that ran the population count.
options.misconception: treats shared authorship as the bridge in the argument

options.text: Wetland drainage is well known to affect amphibians in other counties.
options.misconception: offers a general precedent rather than the bridge

questions.explanation: The warrant is the bridge assumption linking evidence to conclusion: any change after the works was caused by them. The others are cited reasons or background facts, not the connecting assumption.
questions.hint: Ask what assumption makes the reason work.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Unstated premises a reader must supply
questions.learningObjective: Recognise what the argument takes for granted
questions.stem: A survey argues that the marsh is healthy because it holds three species of wading bird. What unstated premise must the reader supply?

answer.exemplar: The argument silently assumes that the presence of those birds indicates habitat quality, and that the birds are sensitive enough to be useful indicators of that quality. It also assumes the count is comparable across years and that the absence of other species is not itself the relevant fact. A reader who accepts only that some birds are present, without the indicator assumption, has no reason to accept the health conclusion, which is why the survey must state the missing premise rather than leave it to the reader.

questions.explanation: The hidden premise is that these birds indicate marsh condition, and the argument needs it because a count alone says nothing about habitat quality. Doubting the link removes the conclusion.
questions.hint: Ask what the bird count would have to show to prove health.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a summary that preserves the argument's structure
questions.stem: Explain what makes a summary of a survey report preserve the structure of the original argument.

answer.exemplar: A summary preserves structure when it keeps the links between the reasons and the conclusion, not merely the list of findings. If the report argued from three counts to a conclusion about site condition, the summary must keep those three counts in the role of reasons and must not promote one of them into a conclusion of its own. A test is whether the summary still makes the original inference available: a reader who only reads the summary should be able to see why the conclusion was drawn, not merely that it was drawn.

questions.explanation: A summary preserves structure when it keeps the links between the reasons and the conclusion, so a reader can still see why the conclusion followed. Findings kept without that role become a list.
questions.hint: Check whether the why survives the compression.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Decide which of two readings the survey supports
questions.stem: Explain how a survey team should adjudicate between two readings of the same field evidence.

answer.exemplar: The team should write down what each reading predicts would be found if it were right, then look for observations that differ between the two predictions and go and check those. Where the readings make no differing prediction, the disagreement is not settled by evidence and should be recorded as a limit rather than resolved by preference. Where they do differ, the observation that discriminates between them should be made before the report is written, and the result stated plainly in terms of which reading it supports.

questions.explanation: Two readings are adjudicated by deriving a discriminating prediction from each and testing it. If both predict the same observations, the evidence cannot settle the dispute, so state the limit.
questions.hint: Ask which observation would come out differently.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Recognise an inference the evidence cannot support
questions.stem: Explain how a reader can tell that a survey conclusion does not follow from the reasons given for it.

answer.exemplar: The reader should state the conclusion in a form that could be true or false, then write down what would have to be the case for the reasons to support it, and check each of those against the reasons as given. Where a required link has no supporting reason, the conclusion is unsupported, no matter how carefully the observations were recorded. A second check is to ask whether the conclusion is stronger than the evidence permits, for example generalising from four ponds to the whole county or claiming a cause from a correlation observed once.

questions.explanation: A conclusion fails to follow when a link it needs has no supporting reason, or claims more than the observations allow. Careful records do not repair a missing link, nor does precision extend it.
questions.hint: Write what the conclusion requires, then look for it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The warrant joining claim to reason
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the reasoning that connects claim and reason
questions.stem: Explain what a warrant is and what it contributes to an argument in a survey report.

answer.exemplar: A warrant is the assumption that connects a stated reason to the stated conclusion, and it is the part of the reasoning that usually goes unsaid. In a survey report, the reason might be that one pond held breeding newts while two did not, and the conclusion that emergent vegetation matters. The warrant supplies the bridge: ponds without emergent vegetation cannot hold breeding newts. Naming the warrant matters because a reader who rejects it can still accept the reason and the observation, which is exactly the disagreement a report should be able to expose.

questions.explanation: A warrant is the assumption connecting a stated reason to a stated conclusion, and it is the part that goes unsaid. Naming it matters because a reader who rejects it can still accept the observation.
questions.hint: Ask what assumption makes the reason work.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Weight carried by primary and secondary sources
questions.learningObjective: Rank the evidential value of the sources cited
questions.stem: Explain why a secondary source can carry less weight than a primary record of the same fact.

answer.exemplar: A secondary source reports what someone else observed or concluded, so it adds a step between the reader and the observation, and at each step something can be lost, rephrased or overstated. A primary record, by contrast, was produced by the person who made the observation and can be inspected in full. The weight of a secondary source therefore depends on how faithfully and completely it transmits the original, which is why tracing a claim back to the primary record is the only way to judge it properly.

questions.explanation: A secondary source adds a transmission step in which the original can be altered, so it carries less weight than the primary record. Its weight depends on how faithfully it reports the observation.
questions.hint: Count the steps between reader and observation.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a reply advances the discussion
questions.stem: Explain how to judge whether a reviewer's objection has actually contributed to a survey report.

answer.exemplar: The test is whether the objection changes the state of the argument: does it reveal a premise the report left unstated, undermine a claim the report makes, or show that a method cannot answer the question asked? If it does, the team has something to correct, and the report can say so. If it does not, then however well written or however senior the reviewer, the objection has not added anything, and treating a rebuke as a contribution is one of the ways surveys stagnate while appearing to be reviewed.

questions.explanation: An objection contributes when it exposes a hidden premise, undermines a claim or shows the method cannot answer the question. Tone, seniority and force of wording do not make it substantive.
questions.hint: Ask what the team would do differently afterwards.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Unstated premises a reader must supply
questions.learningObjective: Make a hidden premise explicit
questions.stem: Explain why leaving premises unstated is a problem for a reader assessing a survey argument.

answer.exemplar: An unstated premise is invisible to the reader, so a reader who rejects it cannot see that the argument fails at that point, and instead attributes the disagreement to the facts or the conclusion, where it cannot be settled. In a survey this matters because the bridging assumptions are usually the contestable ones, such as that a trap catch represents activity, or that absence in a sample means absence on the site. Making them explicit turns a disagreement about the argument into a disagreement about a stated claim, which can be tested.

questions.explanation: A hidden premise cannot be criticised where it sits, so a reader who doubts it misdirects the disagreement onto the facts. Survey arguments rest on contestable assumptions, which need stating.
questions.hint: Hidden premises cannot be argued with where they sit.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a faithful summary from a distorted one
questions.stem: Explain how to tell whether a summary of a survey report has preserved the original argument.

answer.exemplar: Ask what a reader of only the summary could conclude, and then ask whether the original argument would have supported that conclusion with the reasons it gives. If the summary permits a conclusion the original reasoning would not license, or if it has promoted one of the reasons into a conclusion, the structure has been lost. A useful practical test is to reverse the summary and check whether it still reads as an argument rather than a list, because a genuine summary of an argument keeps the sense in which one statement counts as support for another.

questions.explanation: A summary preserves structure when the conclusions it permits are exactly those the original reasoning licensed, with reasons still in their role. Promoting a reason to a conclusion breaks it.
questions.hint: Check what a reader of only the summary could conclude.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Weigh two interpretations of the same evidence
questions.stem: Explain what it means to adjudicate between two incompatible readings of a survey result.

answer.exemplar: Adjudication means deciding between readings by the evidence rather than by preference, and doing it in a way that is visible to others. The team writes down what each reading predicts, identifies whether any observation would come out differently under the two, and then goes and makes that observation or points to one already in the record. If the readings cannot be separated by any available or feasible observation, that is itself the finding, and it should be reported as a limit on what the data can say rather than resolved by authority or preference.

questions.explanation: Adjudication means deciding between readings on the evidence, visibly. When the readings cannot be separated, the honest outcome is a stated limit, and the disagreement itself may be the finding.
questions.hint: Ask which observation would come out differently.

answer.exemplar: The reader should resist the conclusion's authority and go back to the reasons, asking which of them survive once the conclusion is narrowed to the population, the place and the period actually studied. Often the conclusion is not false but simply stated at the wrong scale, and narrowing it to what was measured restores its force without discarding the work. Where no narrowing is possible, the response is to state the limit explicitly, since an overreach invites the whole survey to be dismissed rather than merely corrected.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The warrant joining claim to reason
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the reasoning that connects claim and reason
questions.stem: Explain what happens to an argument when the warrant is made explicit but then rejected.

answer.exemplar: Making the warrant explicit lets the argument be tested at its weakest point, and rejection of that warrant does not destroy the whole argument, it removes the bridge between the reason and the conclusion. The reason can still stand as an observation, and the conclusion may still be true, but it is no longer supported in the way the report claimed. That is a more useful outcome than the hidden alternative, where a reader who doubts the bridge can only object to the conclusion or the facts and the report cannot show which part is at fault.

questions.explanation: A rejected warrant, once stated, removes the bridge between reason and conclusion without destroying either part. The argument is then openly unsupported rather than merely disputed.
questions.hint: Think of the warrant as a bridge that can be inspected.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Unstated premises a reader must supply
questions.learningObjective: Recognise what the argument takes for granted

stimulus.body: The survey found that the moth light trap caught 214 moths on three nights in June. The team concludes that this is a very rich site for moths.

questions.stem: Which premise does the passage in the extract leave unstated?

options.text: That moths are more attracted to lamps than to other surfaces.
options.misconception: supplies a possible background fact, not the missing link

options.text: That a count of this kind indicates how many moths the site supports.
That June is a good month for moths in this district.
options.misconception: supplies a seasonal reason instead of the required link

options.text: That the trap was positioned beside the vegetation being studied.
options.misconception: supplies a method detail that does not bear on the inference

questions.explanation: The conclusion treats the trap count as a measure of the site's moth population, and that link is nowhere stated. Lamp attractiveness, seasonality and trap placement are reasons, not the premise.
questions.hint: Ask what the count is being taken to stand for.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Apply a follow test to a survey conclusion
questions.stem: The report claims that removing the ditch increased frog numbers on the reserve. How should that claim be restated so the reasons support it?

options.text: Frogs prefer managed reserves to unmanaged ones.
options.misconception: replaces one generalisation with a broader preference claim

options.text: Ditch drainage in reserves generally harms frog populations.
options.misconception: generalises from one reserve to a class of reserves

options.text: Reserves with drainage schemes hold fewer frogs than reserves without them.
options.misconception: keeps the comparative form but claims more than was compared

options.text: Frog counts were higher in the section where the ditch was removed than in the section where it remained.

questions.explanation: The restatement that fits the reasons describes what was counted and where, dropping the causal claim the survey cannot support. Preference and broader comparison outrun the recorded counts.
questions.hint: Say what was counted and where, and stop there.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a reply advances the discussion
questions.stem: Which two-stage move turns a reviewer's point into a usable piece of the survey's argument?

options.text: Ask what claim the point bears on, then write that claim into the limitations section.
Repeat the point in the discussion section, then move on to the next review.
options.misconception: preserves the wording without acting on what it implies

options.text: Reply to the point in the same words the reviewer used, then close the exchange.
options.misconception: mimics agreement without identifying any consequence

options.text: Thank the reviewer in the acknowledgements, then leave the text unchanged.
options.misconception: credits the reviewer while changing nothing in the report

questions.explanation: The reviewer's point becomes usable when it is tied to a specific claim and recorded as a limitation. Repetition, echoed replies and acknowledgements leave the report's claims exactly as they were.
questions.hint: Tie the point to a claim and record it.
